headline: Australia's $12.4T super pool will increasingly take companies private, drive governance shifts, and face mounting liquidity pressure as the retiree cohort grows
reasoning: As superannuation funds grow, Andrew Boal argues they will move beyond 5-6% stakes in listed companies and may take some private entirely, giving them decisive influence over director appointments and executive decisions. On the private assets side, he flags liquidity as a key structural risk: unlike listed equities, private market assets cannot be sold quickly, creating tension with the need to pay retirement benefits on demand. Valuation governance of private assets is also a regulatory focus, since fair pricing between departing and ongoing members is critical. Cash flow management is becoming increasingly important as more members enter retirement and benefit payments start to exceed contributions for mature funds. Finally, brand risk is rising in a competitive environment where members can switch funds, meaning reputational damage could trigger sudden cash outflows.
quote: Yes, the regulator has been turning their mind at this of recent times. So yeah, certainly there's a few things going on with private market assets. 1 is liquidity. So as we have more people moving into retirement, those assets aren't as readily saleable as if they're listed on a Stock Exchange where you can sell them not necessarily at the price you want, but you can sell them quickly, whereas private market assets might take a lot longer to sell. So if you're requiring to payout benefit payments to members at a moment's notice, then liquidity becomes a big issue for funds to manage. And then at the same time, we've all got to sort of think about the private market businesses, how much that's going to to control the diversification of the portfolio and the liquidity requirements then for the the cash flows into retirement. So the governance around private market assets, the valuations put on them is something that regulators very care because there's got to be fairness between different cohorts of members.
episode_title: Why super’s $12.4T future matters for investors | the advisory

headline: Super funds increasingly likely to take controlling or private stakes in ASX companies as index weights become too small to move the needle on portfolio returns
reasoning: Boal illustrates that for a very large super fund, a 5% stake in an ASX 100 company worth $5 billion represents only about $250 million — less than 1% of the fund's Australian equities portfolio — making the position near-immaterial to overall returns. To achieve meaningful portfolio impact, large funds will need to either take much larger stakes or avoid smaller companies altogether. An extreme consequence could be super funds privatising companies outright by acquiring 100% ownership, posing novel governance challenges. Alongside this, super fund voting power will increase substantially, giving them greater sway over director and executive appointments and key corporate decisions.
quote: So at the moment the ASX 100 stock is about $5 billion. And so if a superannuation fund wanted to invest 5% of its money into that, that will be about $250 million. And for a very large fund, that will be less than 1% of its Australian equities portfolio. So it doesn't necessarily make much of an impact on its returns across the whole portfolio. So increasingly, to have a meaningful impact on their portfolio returns, they'll want to take a much larger stake in those companies or ignore them all together. Now if they take a much larger stake, what we might even see happen is that they take some of the company's private by owning 100%, not just 5 or 6%. And so certainly that's one governance issue that we have to think about, but also just the stewardship. They're going to have to be voting more and more. Their votes will mean more for the appointment of directors, the appointment of the executives and all the decisions made by those businesses will have much greater input from superannuation funds.

headline: Australia's super system projected to triple from $4.5T to $12.4T by 2045, lifting pension assets to ~180% of GDP and making Australia the world's second-largest pension system by 2031
reasoning: Andrew Boal explains that the Australian superannuation system is still maturing because many members have only been contributing at the 9% rate since 2002 and won't reach retirement age until the 2040s. This demographic trajectory drives the projected growth from $4.5 trillion to $12.4 trillion. As a proportion of GDP, pension assets will rise from ~150% to ~180%, and Australia is expected to become the second-largest pension system globally by 2031 — a remarkable position for an economy that is far from the second-largest. The upside is reduced reliance on the aged pension, which Boal projects will cost the taxpayer less than 2% of GDP, compared with above 10-15% in some European nations.
quote: Our pension systems now just under 150% of GDP and it's growing to grow to 180% of GDP by within 20 years. And at the moment I think in about 20, thirty, 2031, we'll become the second biggest pension system in the world. But we're certainly not the 20, the second biggest economy in the world. So we're certainly batting above our weight in terms of the size of the pension assets we've grown, which means that it's fantastic because we're now won't be as heavily reliant on the aged pension to help people live better in retirement. So we've set aside this money when you're going to have the cost of the aged pension is going to cost the taxpayer less than 2% of GDP over the next decades, whereas other countries overseas in Europe and elsewhere, it's going to cost above 10%, some approaching 15% of GDP.

headline: Ageing population and shift from accumulation to drawdown will erode the tax base as a growing share of super assets become tax-free in retirement phase; the $3M account cap a policy response
reasoning: As more Australians move from the accumulation phase (where investment earnings are taxed at 15%) into retirement or pension phase (where earnings are tax-free), a growing proportion of the $12 trillion pool will attract no tax. This structural shift reduces government tax revenue from investment earnings. The $3 million cap on concessional account balances was introduced precisely to limit the extent of tax-free treatment at the top end, reflecting the tension between incentivising retirement savings and protecting the tax base.
quote: When you're saving for retirement, the investment earnings on your assets are taxed at 15%. But once you go into the retirement or pension phase, they become tax free. And so as a greater proportion of the population moves into the retirement phase as you suggest and the assets that they hold individually become much load larger as the system continues to mature, then we're going to see a much larger proportion of those assets being tax free in the in the funds hands. And that's why we've seen things like the $3,000,000 cap on account balances to try and put a cap on those concessionary treatment of those investment earnings.

headline: Concentration risk rising as top 12 super entities already control ~80% of APRA-regulated AUM; governance scrutiny will intensify as power consolidates
reasoning: Boal notes that the number of superannuation funds has been shrinking through consolidation, leaving the largest 12 entities accounting for about 80% of APRA-regulated assets under management. As the pool grows to $12 trillion concentrated in a small number of entities, their influence over the companies they invest in will increase substantially. This raises important questions about how regulators and governments ensure these entities act in members' best financial interests, and how stewardship and governance obligations are discharged.
quote: At the moment, the largest 12 superannuation entities account for about 80% of APRA ventilated assets under management. So it's already becoming quite concentrated in a dozen or so very large funds. And as you can see, when the market, when it's the size of the market gets to $12 trillion, that's going to be a lot of capital tied up in a small number of entities. So they're going to wield a lot of power in that regard and so it's going to become increasingly important as to how they manage the entities they invest in and how the regulators and the governments make sure that they're acting in the members best financial interests.

headline: Australian super funds have shifted from predominantly domestic to increasingly global allocation as the pool has outgrown local market capacity
reasoning: Boal points out that 30 years ago Australian super funds typically held less than 30% of assets offshore, with the majority in domestic assets. As the pool has grown it has increasingly had to look offshore for investment opportunities that can generate the returns needed to act in members' best interests. This trend is expected to continue as the pool grows to $12 trillion, meaning Australian capital will have an ever-larger footprint in global markets.
quote: When we look at how superannuation funds invest, you go back 30 years or so and they always typically invested around less than 30% offshore. Mostly the assets were held in Australian assets, but as they've grown they've increasingly had to look elsewhere for opportunities to invest the money to achieve the returns necessary to act in their members best interests.
